entries.name: Gumbel-Top-k trick
entries.definition: A categorical sampling construction that adds independent standard Gumbel noise to each category’s log weight and returns the indices of the k largest perturbed values in descending order, producing an ordered sample without replacement under successive renormalization of the remaining weights.
entries.identity_notes: This is the finite categorical Gumbel-Top-k construction formalized by Kool and colleagues, who credit an earlier observation by Vieira. The k=1 case is the Gumbel-Max trick. It is distinct from truncating a language model to its k most probable tokens and then sampling, from a continuous Gumbel-Softmax relaxation, and from the separate stochastic beam algorithm that applies the construction implicitly to sequences. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 328 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in worktree and main, returning 49 and 49 lines respectively. All 2 unique hit contents were inspected: a saved stochastic-beam/Gumbel discovery lead and a search-result title about coalition-formation scatter search, not existing candidate records. Exact checkout counts and differences are retained in the ledger. Nine exact AIO CLASS nodes with scoped synonyms/comments and outgoing edges and four full native neighboring records were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.
limitations: The ordered sampling probabilities differ from marginal inclusion probabilities; inclusion is not generally proportional to the original weight or equal to k times its normalized probability. At k=n every supported category is included.

The stated construction assumes positive finite weights and k no larger than the positive support. Zero weights require exclusion or a declared limiting convention; invalid weights and k beyond support are not covered.

Exactness assumes the specified independent continuous noise and exact ranking. Finite precision, random-number endpoints and numerical ties require implementation policies; no software implementation was certified.

Direct finite-domain application perturbs all n category scores. It does not by itself supply an efficient algorithm for exponentially many complete sequences, a differentiable relaxation, or an unbiased sample-mean estimator for arbitrary without-replacement outputs.

claims.statement: For n categories with positive finite weights w_i and 1≤k≤n, draw independent G_i with the standard Gumbel distribution, equivalently G_i=−log(−log U_i) for independent U_i uniform on (0,1). Rank log(w_i)+G_i and return the first k distinct indices in that perturbed order. The probability of an ordered distinct tuple (i_1,…,i_k) is the product over j of w_i_j divided by the total weight remaining after indices i_1,…,i_(j−1) are removed. Common weight normalization is unnecessary because it adds only a common shift to all log scores. This is an exact distributional statement for the specified random variables, not an assertion that the selected indices are the highest-probability unperturbed categories.

entries.name: Stochastic beam search
entries.definition: The sequence-sampling algorithm of Kool, van Hoof and Welling that implements Gumbel-Top-k without replacement implicitly on a locally normalized sequence tree by propagating conditional perturbed subtree maxima and retaining the k highest-scoring prefixes at each level.
entries.identity_notes: This record denotes the 2019 Gumbel-based sequence sampler, not every search algorithm called stochastic beam search. The generic Gumbel-Top-k distributional construction is a separate record. The method differs from independently resampling prefixes at every beam step, ordinary probability-ranked beam decoding, and diversity-penalized beam groups. An earlier search hit about coalition-formation scatter search is a separate title lead, not evidence of equivalence. limitations: The requested sample count must not exceed the number of positive-probability complete leaves. Zero-mass branches require exclusion or an explicit limiting representation; an exhausted support is not a source of additional distinct samples.

The exact sampling statement requires consistent conditional subtree maxima and the declared normalized sequence distribution. Independently resampling prefixes at each depth, using raw length-normalized scores, or transplanting ordinary beam early stopping does not inherit that statement.

The paper assumes common-length sequences with padding possible. Variable-length generation requires an explicit terminal/EOS policy preserving the intended leaf distribution; arbitrary forced truncation or nonterminating probability mass is not silently covered.

The linear-in-k-and-length claim concerns the number of model evaluations. Vocabulary expansion, top-k selection, neural-state storage and numerical operations still have costs; this is not a bound independent of vocabulary size or model cost.

The conditional-maximum formula can be numerically unstable in direct exponential form. Appendix B supplies stable transformations; exact distributional reasoning is not a certification of finite-precision implementation.

Distinct complete samples can share prefixes and need not have high semantic diversity or be the unperturbed MAP sequences. Without-replacement samples are dependent, and arbitrary unweighted sample averages are not automatically unbiased.

claims.statement: Represent complete sequences as leaves of a finite locally normalized prefix tree, using a declared common horizon or probability-preserving padding of completed sequences. A prefix log probability is the log of its descendant probability mass. Its stochastic score represents the maximum perturbed leaf log probability in that subtree. Start at the root; its maximum may be sampled from Gumbel(0) or fixed at zero as in Algorithm 1, since the maximum is independent of the selected ranking. For each retained parent with stochastic score T, sample independent child values G_i from Gumbel(phi_i), where phi_i is the child’s cumulative log probability; let Z=max_i G_i, then transform each to −log(exp(−T)−exp(−Z)+exp(−G_i)). This samples child maxima conditionally on their maximum being the parent’s T. Pool child candidates and retain up to k with the largest transformed scores, repeating through the declared horizon. Under the stated finite normalized tree construction this returns the same ordered without-replacement sequence distribution as explicitly applying Gumbel-Top-k to all complete leaves. The ordering is by perturbed score, not raw sequence probability.

entries.name: Diverse beam search
entries.definition: The inference procedure of Vijayakumar and colleagues that partitions a sequence beam budget into groups and updates each group using model log-probability scores augmented by a weighted dissimilarity to the already-updated earlier groups at the same decoding step.
entries.identity_notes: This record denotes the group-based diversity-augmented method published at AAAI 2018, first submitted under a different title in 2016. It is distinct from Gumbel-based stochastic beam sampling, inter-sibling rank penalties, repeated complete beam runs with final-output diversity, and earlier algorithms using the phrase diversity beam search. The diversity objective is integrated into group beam updates; the procedure requires no retraining of the scoring model. limitations: The first group is an ordinary beam of width B′. Its baseline inclusion is not a guarantee of matching or beating an ordinary beam of total width B, nor a guarantee of global MAP or globally optimal diversity.
Setting G=1 recovers an ordinary width-B beam. With G>1, setting lambda=0 leaves separate smaller beams; it does not generally reconstruct one width-B beam and can reproduce outputs across groups.

Distinctness is enforced within each selected group. The soft inter-group diversity term does not impose hard global output uniqueness, semantic correctness or a minimum pairwise distance. Large diversity weight can overwhelm model scores.

The diversity measure and strength, group allocation/order, score ties, EOS handling and maximum length are part of the configuration. Prefix-based diversity cannot automatically use an arbitrary sentence-level metric that requires completed outputs.

The paper reports empirical quality/diversity gains in specified generation experiments. No universal superiority, runtime speedup, numerical benchmark result or current library behavior is asserted here.

claims.statement: Divide a total beam budget B into G ordered groups, conventionally each of width B′=B/G when divisible; the paper also allows unequal allocations. At each decoding step, update the first group by ordinary beam search. For every later group in order, extend its retained prefixes by one token and score each candidate by its cumulative model log probability plus lambda times its dissimilarity to the current-step beams already selected in all earlier groups, with lambda nonnegative. For the additive family, dissimilarity to a group is the sum of pairwise sequence dissimilarities. Select the group’s top B′ distinct candidate extensions under that augmented score and proceed to the next group. Repeat through the chosen maximum length or termination condition, then combine group outputs and sort by model log probability as described in the source prose. The method is greedy across both time and group order; it encourages diversity between groups rather than imposing a joint exact sequence-set optimum.

claims.statement: The source’s simple Hamming-style option penalizes a candidate token according to how often earlier groups used that token at the same position. native_neighbors.name: Breadth-first beam search
native_neighbors.definition: A heuristic search procedure that advances by depth layers, retaining at most a chosen beam width of the best-ranked candidate nodes for each next layer and discarding the other candidates.
native_neighbors.identity_notes: This record denotes the conventional breadth-first form of beam search. Wider historical uses of beam search also include global best-first frontier truncation and other heuristic pruning procedures. A width of one follows a single surviving continuation; it is not the unbounded global-frontier algorithm curated as greedy best-first search. No normalized identity match was found across the 442 AIO and 130 prior native records; ignored-inclusive text hits in the main checkout were prior discovery leads, source citations and search-order contrasts, plus incidental lightbulb and wet-bulb dependency substrings, not existing concept records.
limitations: Width pruning can discard every path to a solution or every optimal path, so basic beam search has no general completeness or optimality guarantee.
A layer-width bound does not by itself bound all memory: stored predecessor information, retained earlier layers, generated successors and any global duplicate table must also be accounted for.

Ranking, ties, goal stopping and duplicate handling are additional choices. Increasing the beam width does not guarantee an improvement in returned solution quality for every implementation and problem.

native_neighbors.name: Vanilla sequence beam decoding
native_neighbors.definition: A layer-based sequence beam decoder in which completed and unfinished hypotheses compete for the same k beam slots: finished hypotheses are carried forward unchanged, unfinished hypotheses are extended, and the top-scoring candidates form the next beam.
native_neighbors.identity_notes: This is the vanilla sequence-decoding policy contrasted with FCFS by Kasai and colleagues. It specializes generic breadth-first beam search by specifying EOS retention and competition for active slots. Finished outputs are not accumulated in a separate permanent set, and the procedure is not the score-prioritized per-length best-first decoder. No normalized identity match was found across the 442 AIO and 141 prior native records; ignored-inclusive text hits in the main checkout were prior discovery leads and incidental substrings such as builds in records, source text and dependencies, not existing concept records.
limitations: A completed hypothesis can later fall off the beam because it competes with unfinished candidates. Its discovery alone does not reserve an output slot.
Finite beam pruning is not exact global MAP decoding. Different tie, length-score and maximum-length policies can change outputs.
At the length limit, an implementation must specify what to return if no retained hypothesis is EOS-complete; the simplified figures do not provide a universal failure policy.

Figure 2 in the 2024 paper omits initialization/reset of its temporary H pool. The fresh-per-layer interpretation is supported by the layer-based prose and the explicit reset in Meister et al. 2020 Algorithm 1; the record does not certify the 2024 figure as executable code.
The name identifies the source-defined policy, not a claim that all libraries or all uses of beam search implement it.

native_neighbors.name: Beam decoding with a monotone-score stopping certificate
native_neighbors.definition: A layer-based sequence beam decoder that retains the best completed hypothesis seen so far and stops when the highest current prefix score cannot exceed that incumbent under a score that never increases with extension.
native_neighbors.identity_notes: This is Huang, Zhao and Ma’s 2017 optimal-ending procedure, with optimality explicitly limited by the retained beam. It differs from stopping on a completed top-ranked item without remembering earlier completions, from counting completed outputs, and from score-prioritized best-first expansion with per-length budgets. No normalized identity match was found across the 442 AIO and 146 prior native records; both checkout text searches included ignored and hidden files and returned no matches for the selected exact IDs, full labels, aliases and source titles.
limitations: The certificate concerns descendants of retained beam prefixes. It does not recover prefixes pruned by finite width or guarantee global MAP decoding.
A non-increasing extension score and a stored completed incumbent are required. Length normalization or positive rewards can invalidate the raw-prefix bound and need a different certificate.
The paper compares stopping times under the same beam evolution and a specific historical top-completed baseline. It does not establish universally fastest decoding or current software defaults.
Better model score does not imply better translation quality; the source reports short-output problems under pure probability scoring.
Finite resource limits, absent EOS completions, empty beams and tie conventions need explicit implementation policies. No unconditional finite-time termination claim is made.

definition_evidence.locator: Sections 2–3, Equations (1)–(2), Theorems 1–2, printed p. 2135 / PDF p. 2

claims.statement: Expand the current beam by one token and retain the highest-scoring candidates under a fixed beam policy. Do not extend EOS-complete hypotheses. Maintain the best completed hypothesis encountered in retained beams. Once that incumbent exists, stop when the maximum current prefix score is at most its score. Products of conditional probabilities in [0,1], or their cumulative log probabilities, cannot increase with extension, so descendants of retained active prefixes cannot improve the incumbent when the inequality holds.
